vignette:
Kofi is a 30-year-old Ghanaian-American man who works as a curriculum designer for a mid-sized educational nonprofit in Atlanta. He presents as soft-spoken and carefully composed, though the effort that composure requires becomes apparent over the course of the first few sessions. He sought help after a colleague noticed him standing frozen in the office kitchen, unable to move, following a moment he could not easily explain.

The relationship had lasted fourteen months. His former partner's abuse was not constant - it arrived in cycles, punctuated by periods of warmth that Kofi now understands were part of the pattern, though understanding this has done little to diminish the damage. The worst incident occurred on a Saturday evening when his partner had been drinking heavily. Kofi remembers the smell of alcohol on his breath before the first blow, and the acrid, burning smell that drifted in from something left too long on the stove - a detail that lodged itself in his nervous system with a precision his conscious mind could not have managed. He was struck repeatedly, mostly to the face and torso. He remembers lying on the floor, certain he was going to be seriously hurt, the terror absolute and unambiguous. His partner said nothing was going to happen to him and laughed. Kofi did not call the police. He left the apartment the next morning and never returned. Nothing formal was ever done.

In the months that followed, his body did not allow him to simply move on. When the memories return - and they return without warning - Kofi does not experience them as recollections. He feels them. A dull, pressured ache spreads across his ribs and jaw, the same places that absorbed the blows, and the terror he felt on that floor reconstitutes itself with an immediacy that leaves him gripping the edge of whatever surface is nearest. These memories carry their own sensory world: he can sometimes smell both the alcohol and the faint burn, even in a clean, quiet room. And it is precisely this quality of the memories - their physicality, their insistence on the present tense - that makes certain moments in his daily life so treacherous. The smell of alcohol at a work social event, or the burnt odour from a toaster in the office break room, does not remind Kofi of what happened. It returns him there, pulling the full memory forward with a force that bypasses any intention he has to stay grounded in the present. Even a colleague's offhand comment about family - the kind of remark that would pass unnoticed in any other context - can be enough, because his partner had frequently invoked Kofi's family during episodes, weaponising them, and those associations are now embedded in the architecture of his fear.

What makes this harder still is what these intrusions confirm to him about himself. Each time a trigger pulls the memory forward, and each time the memory surfaces on its own, Kofi is left with a set of convictions that have grown more entrenched over time. He had come to believe, with a quiet but immovable certainty, that the person he was before - curious, socially at ease, someone who trusted his own judgment - no longer exists. What replaced him is someone he does not recognise and does not particularly like. He is also haunted by a sense of injustice that has no outlet: what was done to him was real, it was serious, and it was never acknowledged by anyone with the authority to name it as wrong. Beneath both of these runs something more visceral - a feeling of contamination, as though the abuse left something on him that ordinary living cannot wash off. These appraisals are not beliefs he holds abstractly; they are conclusions the memories keep re-teaching him, and the triggers keep re-confirming.

At work, Kofi has quietly reorganised his days to avoid the kitchen between ten and noon, when colleagues tend to gather there with coffee and conversation. He has declined three team lunches. His manager has noticed he seems withdrawn, and a project review was recently delayed because Kofi had not been able to concentrate long enough to finish the accompanying documentation.

What finally brought him in was not the incident in the kitchen, exactly, but what he thought afterward: that he had no idea how to get himself back, or whether there was anything left to return to. What he is most afraid of is that the contamination is permanent. What he is most hoping for - though he struggles to say it directly - is that someone will tell him it is not.
